blocks.text: Of the hundreds of millions of sperm deposited in the vagina, only a few hundred reach the oocyte, and just one is allowed to enter. Within about a day that single sperm has triggered a chemical lockdown of the egg, a restart of its arrested division and the first step of a new genome. How is entry controlled, and what happens in the week that follows before the embryo implants?

blocks.markdown: **Where and when.** The oocyte is ovulated, arrested in metaphase of meiosis II, surrounded by the **zona pellucida** (a glycoprotein coat) and a layer of follicular cells, the **corona radiata**. It is swept into the uterine tube and fertilisation normally occurs in the **ampulla** of the tube within about 24 hours of ovulation. Sperm are not able to fertilise immediately after ejaculation: during several hours in the female genital tract they undergo **capacitation**, in which glycoproteins and seminal proteins are removed from the sperm surface and the sperm becomes hyperactive and competent to undergo the acrosome reaction.

blocks.title: Acrosome reaction
blocks.text: The acrosome is a cap-like vesicle over the head of the sperm containing hydrolytic enzymes (including hyaluronidase and acrosin). When a capacitated sperm binds to a species-specific zona pellucida glycoprotein (ZP3), the acrosomal membrane fuses with the sperm plasma membrane and the enzymes are released. This is the acrosome reaction, and it allows the sperm to digest a path through the zona pellucida.

blocks.markdown: **Steps of fertilisation.** (1) Sperm pass through the corona radiata, helped by hyaluronidase and by the movement of the tail. (2) The sperm binds to the zona pellucida (ZP3) and undergoes the **acrosome reaction**. (3) Acrosomal enzymes digest a track through the zona and the sperm reaches the oocyte membrane. (4) The plasma membranes of the sperm and oocyte fuse and the sperm nucleus and tail enter the oocyte. (5) Entry triggers the **cortical reaction**: cortical granules beneath the oocyte membrane release enzymes into the perivitelline space, altering zona glycoproteins so that other sperm cannot bind (the *zona reaction*), preventing **polyspermy**. (6) The oocyte completes meiosis II, extruding the **second polar body**, and its nucleus becomes the **female pronucleus**; the sperm nucleus decondenses as the **male pronucleus**. (7) The pronuclei replicate their DNA and the parental chromosomes assemble on a common spindle at the first mitotic division, forming the diploid **zygote**. The consequences of fertilisation are restoration of the diploid number (46), determination of the chromosomal sex (X or Y from the sperm), and initiation of cleavage.

blocks.title: Tracking chromosomes through fertilisation
blocks.prompt: An ovulated oocyte is arrested at metaphase of meiosis II. Describe its chromosome content before and after sperm entry, and state what the zygote contains.

steps.text: Before sperm entry the secondary oocyte has 23 chromosomes, each still made of two sister chromatids, because meiosis II is arrested at metaphase.

Sperm entry triggers completion of meiosis II: sister chromatids separate, one set is extruded in the second polar body, and the remaining set forms the female pronucleus with 23 single-chromatid chromosomes.
The sperm contributes a male pronucleus with 23 chromosomes.
Both pronuclei replicate their DNA, and the zygote is diploid with 46 chromosomes; it then undergoes its first mitotic division.

blocks.answer: The zygote is diploid (46 chromosomes), formed by fusion of a 23-chromosome female pronucleus (after meiosis II is completed) and a 23-chromosome male pronucleus.

blocks.markdown: **Cleavage.** After fertilisation the zygote undergoes a series of rapid mitotic divisions called **cleavage**, as it travels along the uterine tube. There is no growth between divisions, so the daughter cells (**blastomeres**) get smaller with each division while the total volume of the embryo, still enclosed in the zona pellucida, stays about constant. At about the 8-cell stage the blastomeres flatten against each other and become tightly bound (**compaction**), forming an inside cell group and an outside cell group. At about 16 cells (day 3) the solid ball of cells is called the **morula**. The morula enters the uterine cavity at about day 3-4.

**The blastocyst.** Fluid passes into the morula and forms a cavity, the **blastocoele**. The embryo is now a **blastocyst** (day 4-5), with two cell populations: the **inner cell mass (embryoblast)**, which will form the embryo, and the outer **trophoblast**, which will form the placental tissues. At about day 5 the blastocyst hatches from the zona pellucida, which allows it to attach to the endometrium. **Implantation** begins at about day 6 as the trophoblast attaches to the endometrium at the *embryonic pole* and differentiates into cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast, which invades the endometrial stroma. The endometrium, under the influence of progesterone, is in its secretory phase and becomes the decidua.

rows: Diploid cell in the ampulla; zona pellucida intact
Blastomeres divide without growth; getting smaller
Solid ball after compaction; enters uterine cavity
Blastocoele with inner cell mass and trophoblast; hatching from the zona

blocks.title: Cleavage without growth
blocks.prompt: A zygote has a volume of $2.0 \times 10^{6}\ \mu m^3$. Assuming that cleavage divisions are synchronous and without growth, what is the average volume of a blastomere after 4 divisions, and how many cells are present?

steps.text: Each division doubles the cell number. After 4 divisions:
Total volume is unchanged, so the average blastomere volume is the total divided by 16:

blocks.answer: 16 cells (the morula), each of average volume $1.25 \times 10^5\ \mu m^3$.

blocks.title: Normal timing keeps the embryo in the uterus
blocks.text: The embryo normally reaches the uterine cavity as a morula around day 3-4 and implants as a hatched blastocyst around day 6. Transport depends on the peristalsis of tubal muscle and the beating of ciliated cells; if transport is delayed, the zona pellucida is lost and the blastocyst can adhere to whatever surface it meets.

blocks.markdown: **Abnormal implantation and ectopic pregnancy.** An **ectopic pregnancy** is implantation outside the uterine cavity. About 95% occur in the uterine tube, most commonly in the **ampulla**, and others occur in the isthmus, the ovary, the abdominal cavity or the cervix. The usual cause is delayed or obstructed transport of the embryo, so risk factors include previous pelvic inflammatory disease, previous tubal surgery or an earlier ectopic pregnancy, and an intrauterine device. Because the tubal wall has no decidual response and is thin, the trophoblast erodes into the wall. Typical presentation is a woman of reproductive age with a missed period, lower abdominal pain and vaginal bleeding, a positive pregnancy test and no intrauterine pregnancy visible on transvaginal ultrasound. Tubal rupture causes life-threatening intra-abdominal haemorrhage. A related abnormal site is implantation low in the uterus, near the internal os, which gives rise to a placenta praevia.

blocks.title: Why does delayed transport lead to a tubal pregnancy?
blocks.prompt: Scarring after infection has damaged the cilia of the ampulla so that the embryo is transported slowly. Explain how this predisposes to ectopic implantation.

steps.text: The embryo normally takes about 3 days to reach the uterus, as a morula, and still enclosed in the zona pellucida, which is not adhesive.
With impaired ciliary action, transport is delayed; by about day 5 the embryo is a blastocyst and hatches from the zona pellucida.
The hatched trophoblast is adhesive and can attach to and invade the tubal mucosa (usually ampulla), producing a tubal ectopic pregnancy.

blocks.answer: Slow transport lets the blastocyst hatch and attach in the tube before it reaches the uterus.

items: Capacitation precedes the acrosome reaction; the acrosome reaction follows binding to the zona (ZP3).
The cortical reaction blocks polyspermy; the second polar body is extruded.
Cleavage divides without growth; compaction at 8 cells; morula about 16 cells; blastocyst with inner cell mass and trophoblast.
Implantation starts about day 6; the usual ectopic site is the ampulla of the uterine tube.

blocks.title: Common confusions
blocks.text: The acrosome reaction occurs at the zona pellucida, whereas the cortical reaction occurs after sperm-oocyte membrane fusion. The inner cell mass becomes the embryo; the trophoblast forms placental tissues.

points: Fertilisation in the ampulla involves capacitation, zona binding, the acrosome reaction, membrane fusion, the cortical reaction and completion of meiosis II to produce a diploid zygote.
Cleavage produces progressively smaller blastomeres, then a morula and a blastocyst with inner cell mass and trophoblast, which hatches and implants from about day 6.
Ectopic pregnancy results from implantation outside the uterus, most often in the ampulla, usually because of delayed tubal transport.

questions.stem: What is the main function of the acrosome reaction?

options.text: Release of enzymes that allow the sperm to penetrate the zona pellucida
Release of calcium to prevent polyspermy
Completion of meiosis II in the oocyte
Fusion of the male and female pronuclei

questions.correctOptionText: Release of enzymes that allow the sperm to penetrate the zona pellucida

distractorRationale.a: Correct: acrosomal hydrolytic enzymes digest a path through the zona.
distractorRationale.b: Blocking polyspermy is the job of the cortical reaction.
distractorRationale.c: Meiosis II is completed in response to sperm entry, not by the acrosome reaction itself.

questions.explanation: After binding to ZP3 on the zona pellucida, the sperm releases acrosomal enzymes such as hyaluronidase and acrosin which digest a path through the zona. The cortical reaction later prevents further sperm entry.

questions.stem: After the first sperm fuses with the oocyte membrane, cortical granules release their contents. What is the consequence?

options.text: The zona pellucida is altered so that additional sperm cannot bind
The sperm acrosome is activated
The blastocoele forms
The oocyte re-enters meiosis I

questions.correctOptionText: The zona pellucida is altered so that additional sperm cannot bind

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the zona reaction prevents polyspermy.
distractorRationale.b: The acrosome reaction happens earlier, at the zona.
distractorRationale.c: The blastocoele forms at the morula stage days later.
distractorRationale.d: The oocyte completes meiosis II; it does not re-enter meiosis I.

questions.explanation: Cortical granule enzymes modify zona glycoproteins so that other sperm cannot bind or penetrate, thereby preventing polyspermy (which would produce a triploid or abnormal embryo).

options.text: A fluid-filled cavity with an inner cell mass and a surrounding trophoblast
A solid ball of about 16 cells within the zona pellucida
A single diploid cell with two pronuclei
A two-layered disc of epiblast and hypoblast with an amniotic cavity

questions.correctOptionText: A fluid-filled cavity with an inner cell mass and a surrounding trophoblast

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the blastocyst has a blastocoele, inner cell mass and trophoblast.
distractorRationale.d: This describes the bilaminar disc, which forms after implantation begins.

questions.explanation: The blastocyst forms at day 4-5 when fluid collects in the morula, creating the blastocoele and separating the inner cell mass from the outer trophoblast.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old woman with previous pelvic inflammatory disease presents at 7 weeks after her last period with unilateral lower abdominal pain and light vaginal bleeding. A urine pregnancy test is positive and transvaginal ultrasound shows an empty uterus. What is the most likely site of the pregnancy?

options.text: Ampulla of the uterine tube
Fundus of the uterus
Wall of the posterior fornix of the vagina
Anterior surface of the liver

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the ampulla is the commonest ectopic site.
distractorRationale.b: The fundus is within the uterus, so it would be visible on ultrasound.
distractorRationale.c: Vaginal implantation does not occur; the cervix and abdomen are rare sites.
distractorRationale.d: Abdominal pregnancies are rare compared with tubal ones.

questions.explanation: Pelvic inflammatory disease damages tubal cilia and mucosa and impairs embryo transport; pain, bleeding, a positive test and an empty uterus indicate an ectopic pregnancy, most often in the ampulla of the tube.

questions.stem: Which statement about cleavage is correct?

options.text: Cleavage divisions are mitotic and each blastomere is smaller than its parent because there is no growth between divisions
Cleavage divisions are meiotic and halve the chromosome number
Each cleavage division doubles the volume of the embryo
Cleavage occurs only after implantation

questions.correctOptionText: Cleavage divisions are mitotic and each blastomere is smaller than its parent because there is no growth between divisions

distractorRationale.b: Cleavage is mitosis; meiosis occurs only in germ cell formation.
distractorRationale.c: The overall embryo volume stays about constant inside the zona.
distractorRationale.d: Cleavage occurs in the uterine tube during the first days, before implantation.

questions.explanation: Cleavage is a series of mitotic divisions in the uterine tube without intervening growth, so blastomeres become smaller while the embryo volume remains approximately that of the zygote.

questions.stem: A zygote has a volume of 8.0 x 10^5 cubic micrometres. Assuming synchronous cleavage with no growth, what is the average volume of one blastomere after 3 divisions? Give your answer in cubic micrometres.
questions.explanation: Three synchronous divisions give 2^3 = 8 cells. Total volume is unchanged, so each blastomere averages 800,000 / 8 = 100,000 cubic micrometres.

questions.stem: True or false: Capacitation of sperm occurs in the female genital tract before the acrosome reaction.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: Sperm must spend several hours in the female tract undergoing capacitation, during which they become able to undergo the acrosome reaction on contact with the zona pellucida.

questions.stem: Outline the sequence of events from the contact of a sperm with the zona pellucida to the formation of the zygote.
markingGuide: Capacitated sperm penetrate the corona radiata and bind to ZP3 on the zona pellucida.
Acrosome reaction: release of hyaluronidase and acrosin that digest a path through the zona.
Sperm and oocyte membranes fuse; sperm nucleus enters.
Cortical reaction alters the zona to block polyspermy.
Oocyte completes meiosis II and extrudes the second polar body; female and male pronuclei form.
Pronuclei combine their chromosomes on the first mitotic spindle to give the diploid (46-chromosome) zygote.
questions.explanation: Fertilisation proceeds through zona binding, the acrosome reaction, membrane fusion, the cortical reaction, completion of meiosis II and pronuclear union.

questions.stem: Describe cleavage and explain how the morula and blastocyst differ in structure and in the fate of their cells.
markingGuide: Cleavage: rapid mitotic divisions without growth, producing smaller blastomeres within the zona pellucida.
Morula: solid ball of about 16 cells (about day 3).
Blastocyst: fluid-filled blastocoele develops; inner cell mass (embryoblast) forms the embryo and trophoblast forms placental tissues.
Blastocyst hatches from the zona at about day 5 and implants from about day 6.
questions.explanation: The morula is a solid cluster whereas the blastocyst has a cavity and two distinct cell populations with different fates.

questions.stem: Explain how implantation in an abnormal site results in an ectopic pregnancy, naming the commonest site and three risk factors, and explain why rupture is dangerous.
markingGuide: Ectopic pregnancy is implantation outside the uterine cavity; commonest site is the ampulla of the uterine tube.
Mechanism: delayed or obstructed transport allows the blastocyst to hatch and attach to the tubal mucosa.
Risk factors: previous pelvic inflammatory disease, tubal surgery, previous ectopic pregnancy, intrauterine device.
Tubal wall is thin and lacks a decidua, so trophoblast invades the wall and can rupture it.
Rupture causes intra-abdominal haemorrhage and hypovolaemic shock, an emergency.
questions.explanation: Delayed transport allows the embryo to become an adherent hatched blastocyst before reaching the uterus. The thin tubal wall cannot support growth so rupture with bleeding may follow.
